Stage 3 · Reading

Believing in the moon

A text that keeps pointing backwards at itself — and a belief that thirty-seven studies could not remove.

🌕🧠
1 · Before you read. Do nurses, police officers and teachers notice more difficult behaviour at full moon?

Choose one and say why. Compare with a partner before you read.Choose one and say why before you read.Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

Believing in the moon

Written for this course, from Rotton & Kelly, ‘Much ado about the full moon: a meta-analysis of lunar-lunacy research’, Psychological Bulletin 97(2), 1985.

1Ask ten people whether a full moon changes the way we behave, and most of them will say that it does. This is one of the most widespread beliefs in the world, and it survives in the absence of any supporting evidence at all. Nurses repeat it; so do police officers, and some of them will tell you that they can feel the difference on a busy night. That feeling is genuine. The pattern behind it is not.

2The checking has been done, and it was done thoroughly. In 1985 two researchers collected thirty-seven published and unpublished studies of the supposed effect and combined them statistically, looking at hospital admissions, crisis calls, homicides and other criminal offences. A few individual results reached statistical significance; almost any large collection of studies will retain one or two of those. But when the whole set was measured together, the phase of the moon accounted for no more than one per cent of the variation in the behaviour usually described as lunacy. The authors advised that further work on the question was unnecessary. Forty years later, the belief is exactly where it was.

3The reason it survives is not complicated. We notice the nights that fit the story and forget the ones that do not. A ward that is unusually lively during a full moon confirms the belief; a quiet one does nothing to it, because nobody retains a quiet Tuesday. Neither praise for the careful studies nor criticism of the sloppy ones has changed a single mind, and it is easy to see why: the belief was never built out of counted evidence in the first place, so counted evidence cannot take it apart.

4Something similar happens with the physical explanation people offer. The moon moves the tides, they say, and we are mostly water, so it must move us as well. This sounds reasonable and is not. Tides are produced by the difference in pull across an entire ocean; on a body the size of a person that difference is smaller than the weight of a drop of sweat. The argument feels scientific because it uses the right vocabulary. That is a different thing from being correct.

5Other beliefs of this kind are stranger. Millions of people are convinced that the 1969 landings were faked, and those who think so usually begin with the same detail: the flag appears to move, and there is no wind up there to make it do so. The explanation is accidental rather than deliberate. The pole was being twisted as it was pushed into the ground, and in the presence of no air to slow the motion, the movement simply continued for longer than it would here. A horizontal rod held the fabric out; that is why the flag looks as though it is flying.

6What all of these have in common is an odd arithmetic. One unexplained detail counts as proof; a mountain of ordinary evidence counts as nothing. For centuries the moon was associated with madness and with evil, and now it is associated with conspiracy instead. The story changes; the shape of the reasoning does not. A cheerful belief and a depressing one turn out to be equally difficult to remove, which suggests that what people are defending is not the claim itself but the pleasure of having noticed something everybody else has missed.

The words that point backwards

4 · One idea, five ways of pointing at it.

1 · Read the explanation.
Pointing backwards without repeating

Written English avoids repeating a noun or a verb phrase, and replaces it with a small word that points back. The reader has to work out what each of these stands for, and almost all difficulty with long texts at this level comes from that job rather than from unknown vocabulary.

Nouns. It and they replace a noun exactly: the story… it. One and ones replace a countable noun when you want to attach something new to it: a busy ward is remembered; a quiet one is not. You cannot say a quiet it. Note also that one is impossible with uncountable nouns: strong coffee and weak coffee, never a weak one.

Whole ideas. This, that, these and those can point at a sentence, an argument or a situation, which it cannot do comfortably: The belief survives without evidence. This is what interests psychologists. This tends to be used for something close or still under discussion, that for something finished or slightly distant.

Verbs. Do so, do it and do that stand in for a verb phrase; do so is the most formal of the three. So do I, so does she, neither do I repeat an action for a new subject, with the auxiliary and the subject inverted. After think, hope, believe and expect, so and not replace a whole clause: I think so, I hope not.

Two more. Such means “of this kind”. The former and the latter pick out the first and the second of exactly two things, and are worth using sparingly: if the reader has to look back, you have saved yourself a word and cost them a sentence.

Synonyms and antonyms in the same job
  • Writers also avoid repetition by changing the word: the belief → the story → the claim → the myth.
  • These are not perfect synonyms: claim is neutral, myth already says it is false.
  • The opposite pair works the same way: praise and criticism, presence and absence, genuine and faked.
  • When you meet a new word for something already named, ask what the change of word adds.

Two things to watch

1 — One cannot replace an uncountable noun. Strong coffee and a weak one is wrong; write strong coffee and weak coffee, or simply a weak cup. The same applies to advice, evidence, information and criticism.

2 — A reference word with nothing to refer to. If a paragraph opens with This shows that… and the previous paragraph contained three ideas, the reader cannot know which one is meant. Add the noun: This absence of evidence shows that… This is the single most useful thing you can do for a reader in your own writing.

11 · Read this before the extra practice.
Every reference word costs the reader a decision

it / they point back to a noun already named: The story is old, and it is still repeated. this / that point back to a whole idea, sentence or situation: Nobody remembers the quiet nights. This is the mechanism. The difference matters. In The report criticised the delay. That was unfair, that is the criticism, not the delay — and if a reader cannot tell which, the sentence has failed.

one / ones replace a countable noun when you want to attach a new description: A busy ward is remembered; a quiet one is not · We keep the nights that fit and forget the ones that do not. They cannot replace an uncountable noun: I need advice — a good one.

Standing in for a verb, and for a whole clause

do so / do it / do that replace a verb phrase. Do so is the formal one (Nothing made the flag move, and nothing needed to do so); do it and do that are the everyday versions.

so do / so does / neither does attach the same action to a second subject, with inversion: Nurses repeat it; so do police officers · The figures show nothing, and neither does the second study. Note the order — auxiliary before subject — and that neither already carries the negative, so neither doesn’t is wrong.

so / not stand in for a whole clause after think, hope, believe, expect, suppose, be afraid: Does it work? I think so · I hope not. such means ‘of this kind’: What such beliefs have in common… the former / the latter pick out the first and the second of two things just mentioned, in that order.

Errors to watch: so does police officers → so do · I think it → I think so · the informations, they are useful → uncountable, so it is useful · a good advice one → one is only for countable nouns.

1 · Read the model.
Model · a local belief, described and examined

Almost everybody in my city believes that you will fall ill if you sit in a draught, and that the illness will be a serious one rather than a cold. This is not a joke told to children; adults rearrange rooms because of it, and a passenger on a bus will close a window in August and expect thanks for doing so. My grandmother believed it, and so does my doctor.

The belief rests on a single kind of evidence: somebody sits by an open window, and two days later they are ill. That sequence is genuine, and it happens often enough to be remembered. The occasions when nothing follows are the ones nobody retains, and there are a great many more of them.

What the research shows is unhelpful for both sides. Cold air does not cause infection, so the strong version of the belief is faked arithmetic; but cold, dry air does make the nose a slightly easier place for a virus to settle, so the weak version is not absurd. Neither the praise of doctors for the second version nor their criticism of the first has reached anybody on the bus.

I have stopped arguing about it. Such beliefs do not survive because people are foolish; they survive because the memorable cases point one way and the absence of a case points nowhere at all.
